sections.h: How Luke begins Jesus' public story (Luke 3–5)
sections.b: Luke dates John's preaching by six rulers, like a Greek historian and like the prophetic books (Luke 3:1–2). He follows Mark's outline (John, baptism, testing, a day in Capernaum, five debates) but reshapes it: John's arrest comes before Jesus' baptism (Luke 3:19–20), the genealogy runs back to Adam and God (Luke 3:23–38), and the rejection at Nazareth, which Mark places later, becomes the opening sermon of Jesus' work (Luke 4:16–30). Luke's own material includes John's answers to crowds, tax collectors and soldiers (Luke 3:10–14), the reading from Isaiah 61 and the miraculous catch (Luke 5:1–11). Characteristic touches appear at once: prayer (Luke 3:21; 5:16), the Holy Spirit (Luke 4:1, 14, 18), "today" (Luke 4:21; 5:26), care for outsiders (Luke 4:25–27) and "repentance" (Luke 5:32).

common: Luke used Mark as a main source and rearranged it, most visibly by moving the Nazareth rejection to the start of Jesus' work.
uncommon: Luke had a separate early source ("Proto-Luke") for the Nazareth scene and the catch of fish, into which he later fitted Mark's material.

sections.h: John in Luke 3: prophet of a changed life
sections.b: Luke introduces John with the formula of the prophets, "a word from God came to" him (Luke 3:2), and quotes Isaiah 40 through to "all flesh will see God's salvation" (Luke 3:6). Only Luke records John's concrete answers to the question "What are we to do?": share tunics and food, collect only what is owed, stop extorting (Luke 3:10–14). The people wonder whether John is the Messiah, and he points to the stronger one who will baptize in the Holy Spirit and fire (Luke 3:15–17). Luke ends John's public story with his imprisonment by Herod Antipas before he tells of Jesus' baptism (Luke 3:19–21), and Josephus confirms both John's preaching and his death at Herod's hands.

common: John was a historical prophet whose baptism Jesus received; Josephus confirms his work and death.
uncommon: Luke placed John's arrest before the baptism to keep John and Jesus in separate eras (Conzelmann).

sections.b: Luke tells Jesus' baptism in a single sentence and puts the weight elsewhere: Jesus is baptized "as the whole people were being baptized," and it is while he prays that heaven opens and the Holy Spirit comes down "in bodily shape, like a dove" (Luke 3:21–22). John's water baptism is "a baptism of repentance, for sins to be forgiven" (Luke 3:3), and John promises one who will baptize "in the Holy Spirit and fire" (Luke 3:16), a promise the risen Jesus repeats and Pentecost fulfills (Acts 1:5; 2:1–4). Josephus describes John's baptism as a purification of the body after the soul had been cleansed by right living.
sections.refs: Luke 3:3; Luke 3:16; Luke 3:21–22; Acts 1:5; Acts 2:38; Acts 11:16

sections.b: John calls for "fruits worthy of repentance" (Luke 3:8) and spells them out for each group that asks, "What are we to do?" (Luke 3:10–14): generosity, honesty, no violence or extortion. Jesus says he has come "to call sinners to repentance" (Luke 5:32); Mark and Matthew lack the last words. Simon's "I am a sinful man" (Luke 5:8) and Levi's leaving everything (Luke 5:28) show what turning looks like. The question "What are we to do?" returns at Pentecost (Acts 2:37), where repentance and baptism bring forgiveness.

uncommon: E. P. Sanders: the historical Jesus welcomed sinners without first requiring the usual repentance and restitution, and Luke's "to repentance" reflects the church's emphasis.

sections.b: Luke's list (Luke 3:23–38) runs upward from Jesus ("People supposed he was Joseph's son") through Nathan son of David, Abraham and Noah to "Adam, the son of God." From Abraham to David it agrees with Matthew 1 and with Ruth 4 and 1 Chronicles 2 (allowing for spellings and the uncertain names Admin and Arni); from David to Joseph it shares only Shealtiel and Zerubbabel with Matthew. It also follows the Greek Old Testament in adding a second Cainan (Luke 3:36; compare Genesis 11:12). Explanations include Africanus' levirate solution, the view that Luke gives Mary's line, the royal-versus-natural-line view, and the critical view that both lists are theological constructions. Richard Bauckham has proposed that Luke's 77 names from Adam to Jesus follow a scheme of weeks of generations.

common: Matthew's and Luke's genealogies differ between David and Joseph, and no explanation has won general agreement.
uncommon: Luke's genealogy is Mary's, with Heli her father.

sections.b: Luke ends Jesus' genealogy with "the son of Adam, the son of God" (Luke 3:38), the only place in the Gospels where Adam is called God's son. The next scene opens with the devil's "If you are God's Son" (Luke 4:3). Many readers see a new-Adam contrast: Adam was tested in a garden over food and fell; Jesus is tested in the wilderness over food and stands. Paul draws the Adam-Christ comparison openly (Romans 5:12–21; 1 Corinthians 15:45). Tracing Jesus to Adam rather than only to Abraham also presents him as belonging to all humanity.
sections.refs: Luke 3:38; Luke 4:1–4; Genesis 2:16–17; Genesis 3:1–6; Romans 5:12–21; 1 Corinthians 15:45

sections.b: In Luke the Spirit keeps leading Jesus "in" the wilderness and the devil tests him throughout the forty days (Luke 4:1–2). The order of the last two tests differs from Matthew's: the kingdoms of "the inhabited world," shown "in a split second," come second, and the temple in Jerusalem last, so the scene ends in the city where Luke's Gospel ends (Luke 4:5–12). Only Luke records the devil's claim that the world's authority "has been handed over to me" (Luke 4:6), and only Luke says the devil left "until his next chance" (Luke 4:13), pointing to Satan's return through Judas (Luke 22:3).

uncommon: Luke pictures Jesus' ministry as a "Satan-free" time between Luke 4:13 and Luke 22:3 (Conzelmann).

sections.h: The devil's claim to the world (Luke 4:6, 13)
sections.b: Showing Jesus every kingdom of the inhabited world, the devil says their authority "has been handed over to me, and I give it to whoever I wish" (Luke 4:6). Some read this as a lie, since God rules the kingdoms (Daniel 4:17); others as a real but borrowed power, matching "this world's ruler" (John 12:31) and the dragon who gives the beast his authority (Revelation 13:2). Jesus disputes not the claim but the price. The devil leaves "until his next chance" (Luke 4:13), and Luke names Satan again when Jesus sees him fall (Luke 10:18), at the bent woman's healing (Luke 13:16) and when he enters Judas (Luke 22:3).
sections.refs: Luke 4:5–13; Luke 10:18; Luke 13:16; Luke 22:3; John 12:31; Revelation 13:2

sections.b: Luke links four mentions of the Spirit in a row: the Spirit comes down on Jesus in bodily shape while he prays (Luke 3:22); Jesus, "full of the Holy Spirit," is led in the wilderness (Luke 4:1); he returns to Galilee "in the Spirit's power" (Luke 4:14); and in Nazareth he reads, "The Spirit of the Lord is on me, because he has anointed me" (Luke 4:18). John had promised one who would baptize "in the Holy Spirit and fire" (Luke 3:16). Acts repeats the pattern for the church: the Spirit comes at prayer, fills believers and empowers them to witness (Acts 1:8; 2:1–4; 10:38).
sections.refs: Luke 3:16; Luke 3:21–22; Luke 4:1; Luke 4:14; Luke 4:18; Acts 1:8; Acts 10:38

sections.b: Jesus' first sermon reads Isaiah 61:1–2 with a line from Isaiah 58:6, announcing "release to the captives" and "a year of the Lord's welcome" (Luke 4:18–19). The Greek word for release, aphesis, is the Septuagint's word for the jubilee (Leviticus 25:10) and Luke's word for forgiveness of sins (Luke 3:3; 24:47). 11QMelchizedek already joined Isaiah 61 to the jubilee laws as a picture of the last days. Readers debate whether Jesus proclaimed a literal jubilee to be practiced (Yoder, Ringe), or used jubilee language for God's age of salvation, or both. Jesus stops before Isaiah's "day of our God's vengeance."

John tells anyone with two tunics to give one to the person with none, and the same with food (Luke 3:11). Jesus' first sermon announces that the Spirit has anointed him "to bring good news to the poor" (Luke 4:18), using the Greek word for the destitute where Isaiah's Hebrew means the afflicted and humble. Luke keeps both senses in view and shows the program at work in healings and the Beatitudes (Luke 6:20; 7:22). Readings range from the spiritual poverty of Matthew 5:3 to liberation theology's preferential option for the poor.
sections.refs: Luke 3:11; Luke 4:18; Luke 6:20; Luke 7:22; Isaiah 61:1; Matthew 5:3

sections.h: The rejection at Nazareth in Luke
sections.b: Luke makes Jesus' visit to Nazareth, "the town where he had grown up," the first scene of his public work (Luke 4:16–30). In the synagogue he reads Isaiah 61 and says it is fulfilled "today." Admiration ("This is Joseph's son, isn't it?") turns to fury when he says no prophet is welcome at home and recalls Elijah and Elisha being sent to foreigners. The townspeople drive him out to the edge of the hill their town was built on to throw him down, but he passes through them and goes on. Mark and Matthew tell a shorter rejection later (Mark 6:1–6; Matthew 13:53–58).

sections.h: Elijah and the widow in Jesus' Nazareth sermon
sections.b: Jesus reminds his hometown that in Elijah's days, when the sky was shut for three and a half years, Elijah was sent to none of Israel's widows but to a widow at Zarephath in Sidon (Luke 4:25–26; 1 Kings 17:8–24). Luke soon tells a matching story: Jesus raises a widow's only son at Nain and "gave him to his mother," Elijah's words in 1 Kings 17:23, and the crowd hails a great prophet (Luke 7:11–17). Luke's Jesus is often compared with Elijah (Luke 9:8, 19, 54).

Jesus' second example is Elisha: Israel had many people with skin disease in his time, "and not one of them was made clean, only Naaman, a Syrian" (Luke 4:27; 2 Kings 5:1–14). Naaman was the commander of an enemy army. Luke later tells of a Samaritan among ten men with skin disease who alone returns to thank Jesus (Luke 17:11–19).

In Nazareth Jesus uses two stories from Israel's own Scriptures, Elijah fed by a widow of Sidon and Elisha healing Naaman the Syrian, to show that God's prophets go where God sends them, beyond Israel's borders (Luke 4:25–27). The anger that follows (Luke 4:28–29) foreshadows the opposition Paul meets in synagogues when he turns to Gentiles (Acts 13:44–50). The point is not that God rejects Israel, but that God's favor cannot be claimed as a possession.

Luke alone says the man was "full of skin disease" (Luke 5:12). He asks to be made clean; Jesus touches him, cleanses him and sends him to the priest with the offering of Leviticus 14, "just as Moses ordered" (Luke 5:14). Leviticus also has the striking rule that a person covered from head to foot is declared clean (Leviticus 13:12–13). In Nazareth Jesus had already recalled Naaman, healed of skin disease (Luke 4:27).
sections.refs: Luke 5:12–16; Leviticus 13:12–13; Leviticus 13:45–46; Leviticus 14:1–32; Luke 4:27; Luke 17:11–19

sections.b: Luke tells Simon's call later and fuller than Mark. Jesus has already healed Simon's mother-in-law (Luke 4:38–39); now he teaches from Simon's boat and tells him to let down the nets. "On your word" Simon obeys, the catch nearly sinks two boats, and he falls at Jesus' knees: "Leave me, Lord, because I am a sinful man." Jesus answers, "Stop being afraid. From now on it is people you will be catching alive," and Simon, James and John leave everything (Luke 5:1–11). The story closely resembles the post-resurrection catch in John 21, where Peter is restored.

Seeing the faith of the friends who lowered a paralyzed man through the roof tiles, Jesus says, "Man, your sins have been forgiven you" (Luke 5:20). The scribes and Pharisees ask who but God can forgive sins; Jesus heals the man so that they may know "the Son of Man has authority to forgive sins here on earth" (Luke 5:24). In Luke forgiveness is a kind of release: the same Greek word aphesis means forgiveness of sins (Luke 3:3; 24:47) and "release to the captives" (Luke 4:18).
sections.refs: Luke 3:3; Luke 4:18; Luke 5:17–26; Luke 7:47–49; Luke 24:47; 2 Samuel 12:13

sections.h: The Pharisees' first appearance in Luke (Luke 5)
sections.b: Pharisees and teachers of the law first appear in Luke as observers who have come "from every village of Galilee and Judea, and from Jerusalem" to hear Jesus (Luke 5:17). In three debates they question his forgiving sins (Luke 5:21), his eating with tax collectors and sinners (Luke 5:30) and his disciples' feasting (Luke 5:33). Luke's portrait is mixed: Pharisees will also host Jesus at dinner (Luke 7:36; 11:37; 14:1), warn him of Herod (Luke 13:31) and, in Acts, defend the apostles and Paul (Acts 5:34; 23:9).

Critics point out that John's disciples and the Pharisees' disciples "keep frequent fasts and offer prayers," while Jesus' disciples eat and drink (Luke 5:33); Luke alone adds the prayers. Jesus answers that the groom's friends cannot fast while the groom is with them, but when he is taken away "they will fast, in those days" (Luke 5:34–35). Acts shows the church fasting (Acts 13:2–3; 14:23), and the Didache sets Christian fast days on Wednesday and Friday.

sections.h: Antipas, Philip and Herodias in Luke 3
sections.b: Luke dates John's preaching by the reigns of two sons of Herod the Great: Herod Antipas, tetrarch of Galilee, and Philip, tetrarch of Ituraea and Trachonitis (Luke 3:1). He then reports in two verses that John rebuked Antipas over Herodias, his brother's wife, and over all his evil deeds, and that Antipas imprisoned him (Luke 3:19–20). Josephus adds that Antipas divorced a Nabatean princess to marry Herodias and later lost a war to her father, which many Jews took as punishment for killing John.

Men serving as soldiers asked John what to do, and he told them not to extort money by force or false charges and to be content with their pay (Luke 3:14). From Augustine on, this verse has been a key text for those who hold that military service is a lawful calling: John did not tell them to leave the army. Peace churches answer that John spoke before Jesus taught love of enemies (Luke 6:27–36) and addressed only the abuse of power; Tertullian already argued that in disarming Peter the Lord disarmed every soldier. See the card on Luke 3.

common: John's words show that soldiering can be done justly.
uncommon: John's words were for people before the kingdom and do not permit Christians to serve in war.

sections.b: Luke alone says heaven opened at the baptism "while he prayed" (Luke 3:21) and that, as crowds grew, Jesus "kept slipping away to the wild places and praying there" (Luke 5:16). These are the first of many such notes: before choosing the Twelve (Luke 6:12), before Peter's confession (Luke 9:18), at the transfiguration (Luke 9:29) and on the Mount of Olives (Luke 22:41). In Acts the Spirit comes on the church as it prays (Acts 1:14; 4:31).
sections.refs: Luke 3:21; Luke 5:16; Luke 6:12; Luke 9:18; Luke 9:28–29; Luke 11:1; Acts 1:14; Acts 4:31

sections.b: Only Luke says that Simon, James and John "left it all behind and followed him" (Luke 5:11), right after the greatest catch of their lives, and that Levi "left everything" at his tax office (Luke 5:28). The theme returns in Jesus' demand to give up all one has (Luke 14:33), the rich ruler (Luke 18:22) and Peter's reminder that they have left their own things (Luke 18:28). Simon's call also begins with fear and a confession of sin, answered by "Stop being afraid" (Luke 5:8–10).
